finalJustifications: Because the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action of Lifecycle removes the unfinished parts after the 7 days — automatic cleaning without touching current uploads.
Because Lifecycle's action automatically completes abandoned uploads, transforming orphan parts into complete objects.

optionReasons.saa-med-200:option:1: Disable logging eliminates day-to-day operational monitoring — the requirement requires you to maintain it.
optionReasons.saa-med-200:option:2: Local logs in instances/Lambda are ephemeral and non-centralised — complete operational regression.
optionReasons.saa-med-200:option:3: It's the closest because you use the right tool (CloudWatch) to react to growth — but alarm + manual exclusion is precisely the human process that Retention Policy eliminates: configured in 90 days, the service expires the old events alone.

finalJustifications: Because the Retention Policy by Log Group (ex.: 90 days) does its own CloudWatch exclude expired events — volume drops and nothing changes in sending application logs.
Because Retention Policy compresses logs with more than 90 days in an archive layer, keeping them accessible for free.
Because Retention Policy exports old logs to the S3 automatically before deleting them from CloudWatch, no configuration.
Because Retention Policy limits the total size of each Log Group, rejecting new events when the ceiling is reached.

finalJustifications: Because SG is stateful (automatic return), but the NACL is statiss: the answers go out to the ephemeral doors of the client, and without the rule of exit the NACL the bar.
Because the NACL process input and output in the same numbered rule, and remove invalid output also input permission.
Because the NACL delegate return traffic to Security Group, which without explicit exit rule discards the answers TCP.
Because the ephemeral door is used by the handshake TLS of the server, and without it the connection does not even establish itself in the entrance.

finalJustifications: Because the CMK with automatic rotation generates new material per year while maintaining the same ARN, and the KMS saves old versions — historical data remain decryptable without redrafting.
Because the CMK with automatic rotation re-crypts the old data in background, updating the objects for the new material.
Because the CMK with automatic rotation emits one ARN new per year and updates application references automatically via alias.
Because the CMK with automatic rotation delegate the old versions to CloudHSM, which preserves the material outside the annual exchange cycle.

optionReasons.saa-med-205:option:3: It's the closest because in simple accounts the IAM policy alone is usually sufficient — but the requirement requires restriction on DUAS layers: to ensure that only that role uses the secret and key, the secret's resource policy and the key policy of the KMS need to name the role; resource policies are not 'optional' when the goal is to stop the resource.

finalJustifications: Because the required control is in double layer: the secret's resource policy restricts the GetSecretValue to the role, and the key policy of KMS restricts the description to the same role.
Because the secret policy resource already spreads permissions to the key policy of KMS, just set up the first of the two.
Because the key policy delegates the decision to the Secrets Manager, which validates the roll once and releases the two operations at once.
Because both policies demand MFA of the instance EC2 each search, and it is the second factor that closes the access of the other roles of the account.

Because the Gateway Endpoint sets up a tunnel TLS dedicated with each pocket, encrypting the traffic that the NAT left it open..
Because the Gateway Endpoint hides the objects of S3 on the edge of the VPC, and most of the readings don't even come out of the local fora network.
Because Gateway Endpoint replaces the NAT Gateway completely, also assuming the rest of the internet traffic of the sub-network.
